Diya lamps flickered along the hostel corridor on the first night of the Diwali break. Sarika sat cross-legged on her bed with her laptop open.
"Peer rating for the design project closes tonight," she said. "I'm giving Kunal a two out of five."
Ishita looked up from folding clothes. "A two? Kunal built the whole prototype in August."
"Yes, but he vanished for the last three weeks. Missed two meetings. I had to finish the slides alone."
"His grandfather was in hospital, remember? And who stayed till midnight fixing the circuit in September?"
Sarika paused, the cursor blinking over the box. "That feels like ages ago."
"It was two good months against three bad weeks."
"Maybe. But the last three weeks are all I can see when I think of him." She sighed and scrolled back through the group chat to August.

qa.q: What rating does Sarika plan to give Kunal?
qa.a: She is giving Kunal a two out of five.

qa.q: Why does a low rating feel fair to Sarika in the moment?
qa.a: She is frustrated and tired after finishing the slides alone, and those last three weeks are so fresh that they feel like the whole story of Kunal's work.

qa.q: What small step would help Sarika rate Kunal more fairly?
qa.a: She could note what Kunal did in each month of the project, from the August prototype to the missed meetings, before picking a number.

qa.q: What would change for Kunal if the rating only counted the last three weeks?
qa.a: His prototype and the late night fixing the circuit would count for nothing, and a hard family time would decide his grade.

grounding: Shows a student letting a teammate's last few weeks outweigh earlier months of good work when rating him.

passage:
Review week in our office always smells of burnt coffee. This year I sat beside Chinmay, our manager, while he prepared for Rukmini's appraisal, and I noticed something odd. He didn't open last month's reports first. He opened a thin notebook with a tab for every month, January to December.
"March: stayed late to rescue the vendor file," he read, half to himself. "July: quiet, but trained two interns."
Rukmini had a rough November; people still talked about the client complaint at lunch. I expected it to sink her review. Instead Chinmay wrote one line about November and four about the rest of the year.
When she came out, she caught my eye and mouthed, "He remembered March, Yash."
I can't say what went on in his head. But I've started keeping my own notebook.

qa.q: What did Chinmay's notebook have a tab for?
qa.a: It had a tab for every month, January to December.

qa.q: What might Yash have felt when Rukmini mouthed that Chinmay remembered March?
qa.a: Yash was probably surprised and reassured, having expected the November complaint to sink her review, and then seeing the whole year counted.

qa.q: What could other managers learn from Chinmay's approach?
qa.a: They could jot a short note every month, so a review weighs the whole year rather than the latest mistake.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see her review if only November had counted?
qa.a: She would likely feel judged by one bad month, with her March rescue and the rest of her year ignored.

grounding: Shows a manager who keeps notes across every month so a performance review reflects the whole year, not only recent memory.

Noor joined Class 4B in January, while paper snowflakes from the winter fair still hung in the school hall. On her first morning she came in late, cheeks red from the cold, and snapped "No!" when Simran offered to share a bench.
"She's rude," Simran told her friends at lunch.
Over the next weeks Noor lent out her glue stick, clapped loudest at the class play and helped Simran pick up a spilled box of beads. Simran mumbled thanks but still whispered, "She's only nice when Miss is watching."
When the teacher paired them for the science chart, Simran's shoulders sagged. Anyone but the rude girl, she thought.

qa.q: What did Noor say when Simran offered to share a bench?
qa.a: Noor snapped "No!" when Simran offered to share a bench.

qa.q: Why does Simran keep calling Noor rude, even after the glue stick and the beads?
qa.a: Simran felt hurt by that first "No!", and now she feels sure she already knows who Noor is, so kind acts look like a show to her.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Simran look past the first day?
qa.a: The teacher could ask Simran to name three things Noor has done since January, like lending her glue stick, and talk about how that first cold, late morning might have felt.

qa.q: What might the first day have been like for Noor?
qa.a: Noor was new, late and cold, so she may have been nervous and snapped without meaning to be unkind, and then found it hard to change how others saw her.

grounding: Shows a child whose first-day opinion of a new classmate stays fixed even when the classmate's later behaviour is kind.

Rain had flooded the road to the placement cell, and the mock interviews were running forty minutes behind. Madhuri, taking notes for the panel, watched Baljeet hurry in, shoes squelching, and apologise three times before he sat down.
The senior on the panel frowned at the puddle and never quite stopped frowning. Baljeet's later answers were sharp, but Madhuri saw the senior write "nervous" in the first minute and underline it at the end.
Outside, she handed him a paper towel. "You were good after minute three. Nobody saw it."
They practised an opening together on the bench: breathe, one sorry, a smile, first answer slow.
In his second slot Baljeet walked in steady. From her corner Madhuri noticed the senior cross out "nervous", pause, and read the whole page again.

qa.q: What word did the senior write in the first minute?
qa.a: The senior wrote "nervous" in the first minute.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling as she watched the senior underline "nervous"?
qa.a: She was likely frustrated on Baljeet's behalf, because she could see his later answers were sharp while the dripping first minute had already decided the note.

qa.q: What small step helped Baljeet in his second slot?
qa.a: Practising a calm opening with Madhuri helped: breathe, one sorry, a smile and a slow first answer.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt leaving the first slot?
qa.a: He probably felt shaken and unsure, knowing he had rushed in wet and apologised three times, even though his answers were sharp.

grounding: Shows a peer noticing how the first minutes of an interview shape the rest, and how a calm opening and a willingness to update both help.

passage:
The first night Diego moved into the flat in Osaka, bass thumped through the thin wall until one in the morning. Yuki lay awake, jaw tight, already composing a cold message.
Instead she opened her notes and typed: "First guess: careless. Only a guess. What would change it? If he turns it down when asked. If he does his share in the kitchen."
The next evening she knocked. "The music carries a lot through this wall." Diego went red, apologised, and bought a pair of headphones that weekend.
Over the following fortnight Yuki kept adding lines: dishes washed, a note on the fridge asking about her shifts, rice left warm for her after a late one.
One night she scrolled back to that first entry, smiled, and deleted the word "careless".

qa.q: What did Diego buy after Yuki knocked?
qa.a: Diego bought a pair of headphones that weekend.

qa.q: How was Yuki feeling that first night, and what did she do with that feeling?
qa.a: She was irritated and tired, lying awake with her jaw tight, but she wrote her judgement down as only a guess and listed what would change it.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Writing "Only a guess" and naming the evidence that would change it worked, because it kept Yuki watching what Diego actually did instead of sending the cold message.

qa.q: What would it have been like for Diego if Yuki had sent the cold message?
qa.a: He might have felt judged on his first night, before he even knew the wall was thin, and the flat could have started with tension instead of warm rice.

grounding: Shows a person treating a first impression as a guess and deliberately watching for evidence that would change her mind.

"You want to know why you still call your eighth birthday the worst one? Sit, Ira. Your Nani remembers it all.
It was the middle of the monsoon. You and Tenzin sailed paper boats in the puddles for an hour, then came the treasure hunt, then the songs. When the chocolate cake came out with sparklers, you shrieked so loudly the neighbours clapped from their balcony.
Then the thunder started, the lights went out, and every parent rushed to take their children home. Tenzin left without saying goodbye. You sat on the stairs crying in the dark.
Next morning you told me, 'The party was the cake and then everyone left.' Three whole hours of fun, and you kept only the sparklers and the stairs."

qa.q: What came out with the chocolate cake?
qa.a: The chocolate cake came out with sparklers.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling on the stairs, and why did it colour the whole party?
qa.a: Ira felt sad and let down when the lights went out and Tenzin left without a goodbye, and because that sadness came last, it pushed out the hour of paper boats and games.

qa.q: When the lights went out, what could have changed how the party was remembered?
qa.a: Someone could have lit a candle, sung one last song and helped Tenzin say goodbye, so the party ended warmly instead of in the dark.

qa.q: How might Tenzin remember the same party?
qa.a: Tenzin may remember the paper boats and the sparklers most, or the rush home in the storm, rather than the stairs where Ira sat crying.

grounding: Shows a child judging a whole birthday party by its exciting cake moment and its sad ending.

passage:
The week before Christmas, fairy lights blinked on every balcony in the Bandra colony, and Aadhya came up to Dilnaz's flat with a laptop full of school trip photos.
"Look, day two, the bonfire! And you on the zipline, screaming."
Dilnaz barely glanced. "That trip was a disaster."
Aadhya kept clicking. Snowball fights on day three. Dilnaz winning quiz night. The two of them sharing hot chocolate at a roadside dhaba.
"You're laughing in every picture," Aadhya said.
"Yes, and then day five happened." Dilnaz pulled a cushion to her chest. The bus had broken down, they had waited six hours in the cold, and her bag had got soaked. "I got home at three in the morning, frozen. That's what I remember."
Aadhya closed the laptop slowly.

qa.q: How long did they wait when the bus broke down?
qa.a: They waited six hours in the cold.

qa.q: Why does Dilnaz call the trip a disaster despite the photos?
qa.a: The cold, soaking six-hour wait on day five was the last and sharpest memory, so Dilnaz still feels miserable about the trip, and the laughing photos feel less real than that night.

qa.q: What could Dilnaz try to get a fairer picture of the trip?
qa.a: She could go through the photos day by day with Aadhya and name one good moment from each day before talking about day five.

qa.q: What is it like for Aadhya when Dilnaz calls the trip a disaster?
qa.a: Aadhya may feel deflated, since she brought the photos to share happy days they had together, and she ends up closing the laptop slowly.

grounding: Shows a teenager letting one bad final day colour the memory of a mostly enjoyable school trip.

passage:
Autumn leaves were piling up outside the laundrette in Lisbon when Camila's message came: the café was turning ten, and old staff were invited.
Amara's thumb hovered, then typed: "No thanks. Worst job of my life."
Camila called straight away. "Worst? You were there three years!"
"You saw my last shift. Senhor Duarte shouting at me in front of customers about the grinder, which I didn't even break. I walked out shaking."
"I saw it. It was unfair. But he also covered your shifts for a month when your mum was in hospital. And who taught you latte art? Who gave us those Christmas lunches?"
Amara went quiet. Those memories were there, but faint, like photos left in the sun. The shouting was still loud.
"I'll think about it," she said, still angry, but less sure.

qa.q: How long did Amara work at the café?
qa.a: Amara was there three years.

qa.q: Why does "worst job of my life" feel true to Amara?
qa.a: The unfair shouting on her last shift was both the most intense moment and the ending, so she still feels angry and humiliated, and three years of kindness look faint beside it.

qa.q: What would you advise Amara before she answers Camila?
qa.a: She could write down both the last shift and the good things Camila listed, like the covered shifts and the latte art, and decide about the party with all three years in view.

qa.q: How does Camila see Amara's time at the café?
qa.a: Camila agrees the last shift was unfair but remembers covered shifts, latte art and Christmas lunches, so to her it was far from the worst job.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose angry final shift at a job threatens to overwrite years of good experiences there.

passage:
The last meeting of the museum guide project in Toronto ran long, and people were already glancing at their coats. Tariq, who led the five-person team, could have ended on the list of bugs still open. He had seen how a final grumble could sour a whole year of work.
So he kept the bugs to one slide, gave each an owner and a date, then clicked to a photo of the team on launch night, grinning under the museum's dinosaur.
"Mei, the map you redesigned in March is why visitors stopped getting lost," he said, and he named one thing for each person.
He finished with, "Monday, fixes. Tonight, go home proud."
Mei lingered by the door. "I thought I'd leave remembering the bugs," she said. "I'm leaving remembering the dinosaur."

qa.q: What photo did Tariq show at the end?
qa.a: He showed a photo of the team on launch night, grinning under the museum's dinosaur.

qa.q: Why did Tariq keep the bugs to one slide?
qa.a: He was worried that ending on a final grumble would sour a whole year of work, and he cared that his team left feeling proud.

qa.q: What made Tariq's ending work?
qa.a: He handled the problems clearly, with an owner and a date for each, then finished on specific praise and a warm line, so the last memory was a good one.

qa.q: What is it like for Mei to hear her March map redesign named?
qa.a: She feels seen and valued, and instead of leaving with the bugs on her mind she leaves remembering the dinosaur photo.

grounding: Shows a leader closing a project on a warm, clear note because people remember the peak and the finish.
